items.title: Welcome to Non-Deterministic Ramblings
items.text: Welcome to this web site, where I hope to be able to record some slivers of wisdom drawn from many years working in IT. Along the way I have met with people and circumstances, many nice but occasionally some not so pleasant, but from each hopefully I have learned something, and if I record it here I hope that you too may find something of value, if only for any humour.

items.title: "Non-Deterministic"
items.text:
A long, long time ago I studied Computer Science, and while I wasn't very good at the wider mathematics courses, I felt a keen affinity with Discrete Mathemmatics. Part of the discrete maths course concerned itself with Non-Deterministic Finite Automata, or NDFA. By all means follow the links for more information, but in those relatively early days, we studied what is now Automata Theory as a precursor to understanding syntax analysis.

For many years, I joked that for all the time we spent studying NDFA I never had one cross my desk, and I think the probable cause which really defines a lot of my reflections in this blog, are that at the time I studied, we did not have the resources to actually build the range of tools we have now that do use state graphs within them.

More recently I have studied Systems Thinking as a post-graduate abd as part of systems modelling we very much get into Determinism. This is when I think of NDFA and smile to myself, as an NDFA as a state machine could not determine an absolutes state given the input. And so it is with my thinking, in producing this blog my ideas seem to go off in myriad directions, rarely taking teh same path twice from any given starting point.

So please excuse the randomness of the pasts, hopefully they do follow in some sort of logical progression

items.title: "Ramblings"
items.text:
Roughly, I have tried to divide the posts on this into under three broad sections

  • Reflecting - We came, we saw, we experienced, and we would like to help you not to fall into the same traps as maybe we did
  • Thinking - in an area dominated by formal certifications and methods, but latterly a paucity of research finding, we develop heuristics that we think may help explain some of the things we see happening in real-world situations
  • Doing - some words about how I have gone about doing some of the IT things I do

I hope that there is something here that will amuse, maybe promote thoughts of your own, and if it does help in any way then my work here is done.

Expressed Views

Please note that all of the views I express on this site are all my own and do not reflect the views of any of my employers past or present

items.title: Russell
items.text:
Despite attempts using AI to make the photo of me look like some sort of secret agent, my career has spanned well over 40 years in and around computing. Starting at a time when it was called Computing, I have worked in Information Technology aka "IT", battled with the Nexus of Forces, and emerged blinking into the light of Digitalisation. EVen now as I write this during summer 2026, the emergence of AI is changing things once again.

I am certainly old enough now that whenever some bright young thing tries to show me something amazing, I can say "Oh we've been able to do that for years ... Nothing New".

Over that time, I started as a programmer, then moved to Product Management, before spending the last 25 years as variously a Solution Architect, an Enterprise Architect, and latterly focussing on Business Architecture. The piece about Purpose of an IT Architect is based upon a myriad of conversations arising from this time.

Academically I have a BSc in Computer Science, an MBA, and an MSC in Systems Thinking in Practice. However despite attending many courses, and passing exams, I am very much in favour of praxis as part of my daily practice.

Hopefully this site contains aspects drawn from a wide variety of experiences. At the top of this site you'll find links to ways to contact me.

items.title: Photographs
items.text:
While I infrequently use images to lighten pages, where I do unless specifically tagged all images are my own. When I remember I shoot with a Panasonic Lumix GX7, otherwise photographs have been captured using my iPhone with either the default camera shipped by Apple, or ProCamera when I am able to master the settings and make it work for me.

At the moment I am using Affinity on my laptop as the image editor.

For many years I have used Paint.NET which is an excellent image editor in my opinion, with a superb set of plug-ins. However it is only available for Windows[61]. I am lucky that in my current job I have access to Paint.NET via the organisations software policy.

I have dipped in and out of usingGimp for many years, and the recent set of add-ons to make Gimp present as much like Adobe as it can is, I think, a big boon for the software. Like a lot of users, I find that my 'muscle memory' for Paint.NET afflicts my use of any other image editor hanse my comments about the Adobe style presentation add-ions for Gimp 3.x.

But to bring this page to a close, I feel that the time has come to address my own 'muscle memory' issue and learn a new image editor. At teh moment, Affinity from Canva is getting rave reviews, and it works well. I particularly like that it combines three tools into one - page layout, vector graphics, and image editing all in one application, it reminds me of the (very) old Windows Works package that combined word processing, spreadsheet, and a rudimentary database, and served me well for wrting my MBA siigenments back in the mid-90s. I digress....

items.title: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold
path: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold

items.title: Bytes, Boards, Boxes
items.text:
In my final year at university studying computer science, there was one lecture that not only made an impression on me at the time, but in the intervening years has stood the test of time and with reflection has increasingly served as a metaphor for life in general.

Delivered as a 50-minute lecture as part of a module on computer architecture, the content has been a major takeaway from my entire degree. I am not aware of wWhether or not this is still taught now as part of any computing related degree, but in my humble opinion it really ought to be as I believe the context holds as true today as it was in early 1982.
path: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold

items.title: A 1982 Approach to architecting computer-based solutions
items.text:
1980s context

At the time of the lecture, there was a lot of compute capability available, both in terms of processor power or memory capability. Our ability to interface computers to the real world was also limited.

The key problem being addressed by this lecture was what is the best way to go about building a system, based around computing hardware, to meet a requirement? One example I saw after university was a hardware design for a firm-control computer for use by artillery.

Given the paucity of developed compute solution as we know them today required a framework for architectural decisions making:

Approach Description Pros Cons Bytes Solution design from individual hardware components Can be made very specific to solving need Difficult to debug / Difficult to customise or update to serve a similar requirement Boards Design based upon a combinations of pre-built boards Boards present pre-debugged chunks of functionality, debug only inter-connections / Potential to repurpose for similar requirements Not as specific to a solution, may require trade-offs in requirements matching Boxes Use a complete, working box for the solution Using a completely debugged solution saves development time Solution may need significant compromises to requirements, or software fixes

The key decision point largely came down to how much time did you have to debug the hardware, Tracey Kidder covered this far better than I ever can in his book The Sould of a New Machine covering teh development of a new computer system, a Box from the components, the Bytes.

My Real-World Example

My first job after university was about addressing the problem of how can we capture and store voice messages? The problem needed to solve some interesting dimensions:

  1. We had to link to a digital telephone line serving voice channels, but the silicon device we had planned for was severely delayed
  2. Storage devices had small capacity, and each voice channels was data intensive1
  3. We needed a general compute server to run a real-time operating system and control everything

The answer we came up with at the time turned out not be a clear cut case of one approach, but a hybrid...

  • There was no box solution, so that was out immediately
  • There were some board solutions available: processor boards, memory boards, storage controllers so they presented a shot cut to the control portion
  • The boards were linked using {Intel Multibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multibus) as a standard interconnect
  • Our plan to use a simple chip for the telephony link had to change to building a board full of chips, and a lot of debugging
  • The research team came up with a compression solution using early DSP ssystem on chip soluions which required their own board ... more hardware debugging
  • All of the above required controlling software
path: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold

items.title: Technically, has 'Bytes - Boards - Boxes' endured?
items.text:
Many technology changes over the intervening forty years have changed the landscape. One irony is that not long after our work in teh example above, a customisable box solution came available which would have saved some of the time we spent simply getting a set of pre-developed boards working together, but we would still have had the other challenges.

My reflection of the changes amounts to:

  • Bytes: Silicon fabrication technology and techniques has created on-chip capabilities way beyond anything we could have anticipated back in 1982, for example a board full of components for a PC board a few years later is now routinely delivered on one silicon component. Our need to string together so many components has reduced.

    More recently the componentization of chiplets and the ability to combine chiplets on a single silicon die has moved the whole Bytes architecture decisions towards the large manufacturers and chip fabricators, as well as raising the economic factors in these decisions.

  • Boards: The original approach of a standard interconnect bus with boards plugged in has been largey left behind by the increasing capabilities available on a singly silicon component. This in turn has created an architecture for Single Board Computers SBC) cards such as the Raspberry Pi.

However, these SBC products have been developed with defined connectivity, such as the General Purpose I/O (GPIO) standard which supports additional plug-in modules, and some development boards for customised hardware solutions.

  • Boxes: The "siliconisation" of components, such as storage devices has merged the distinction between boards and boxes, witness the Raspberry PI as delivering what would previously be a box solution as a standalone single board|

The decision frameworx still endures, but the decision points have moved.
path: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold

items.title: Bytes - Baords - Boxes as a Metaphor
items.text:
The main reason that the lecture has stuck with me reflects my experiences in my roles, and life in general. Whenever solving a problem I tend to think of possible solutions, and the impacts in terms of:

"Bytes" What happens if we put together a lot of different parts to solve our problem. What are the integration challenges (for example, what do i need X to tell Y) An example could be putting my own holiday plans together from teh individual parts "Boards" Are there some integrated parts I can hook into. Using my holiday example, what if I use one company for all my travel needs, flights, car hire etc, and then one hotel chain for different parts of the itinerary? "Boxes" Can I get a single solution with everything pre-integrated? A package holiday? A new build house?
path: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold

items.title: Final Thoughts - Systems Engineering
items.text:
In my practice as an Enterprise Architect, this approach based on Bytes - Boards - Boxes as a metaphor is always part of my toolkit, especially when developing options for stakeholders. In working through teh life-cycle of a project, I can map Bytes - Boards - Boxes metaphor over the Systems ENgineering V Model starting with "Boxes" at teh top level working all teh way down to "Bytes" at the point of the V.

What started as a simple hardware lecture all those years ago has turned into one of the most used tools in the toolbox of my working practice.

  1. Well, 64kbps per channel was deemed very data intensive in the day ↩
path: Does the Bytes, Boards, or Boxes? decision still hold

items.title: WordPress
items.text: I have been endeavouring to create this web site for several years. When doing my MSc, I did create a WordPress site which exists to this day, but it was something that (a) I kept playing with themes of (never being satisfied with a theme), and (b) I struggled t= that every time I returned to create a post that WordPress had changed the writing tools.

items.title: Quarto
items.text:
For various reasons, I ended up using R to do the statistical analysis required for my MSc thesis. THis took me to the Posit tools, notably RStudio.

I was aware of the ability to use RMarkdown as a publishing tool, but cognitively getting my brain around using and publishing made it a step too far at a time when I was trying to learn so many things at the same time

And then Quarto happened... if you haven't seen QUarto from Posit, then it is a well engineered and superbly supported solution, that fits seamlessly into RStudio and so felt very familiar and easy to use (but then RMarkdown was already engineered into RStudio, and so I kink myself that I probably missed a trick there)

So why isn't this site created using Quarto?

Good question! The answer is two fold:

  • Firstly, while the Quarto documentation is excellent as showing how to publish on Posit's own free web hosting, it felt very off the beaten track internet wise.
  • Secondly, Quarto had simply too many options, for me it was back to that cognitive overload, and I seemed to spending way too much time trying to make options that should have worked, work, only to find that under Option A, facility X was not enabled.
  • Thirdly, RStudio takes a bit of getting used to as a serious writing tool. Quarto is very flexible, and the extensive support covers ways to use Quarto withe other IDEs.
  • Finally (this is getting very Monty Python), trying to publish Quarto to GitHub Pages (where you are now) looked quite difficult compared to Posit's won hosting service.

Let me be clear, for serious publishing work, I'd persevere with Quarto as it is just so powerful. Maybe another blog post?

items.title: Zensical
items.text:
And so we arrive at this site, created using Zensical. I heard the lead developer, Martin Donath talking about his work on a podcast. Zensical is a major update to a HTML documentation tool.

So yes, I am still climbing my way up a steep learning curve, but I got in the ground floor when, compared to Quarto, Zensical is relatively simple. And more importantly, the publishing to GitHub Pages is pretty well documented, hence my arrivel here.

It hasn't been plain sailing, again maybe another blog post

items.text:
I guess there are some products that stand as good exemplars of the history of an aspect of computing. Come the Internet age, which started in my household somewhere in teh early 1990s with a dial-up AOL connection alongside a freeware PC TCP stack, and a very early copy of NetScape Navigator. Having plugged it all together, whether physically, or software-wise, it took three attempts to reach the web site of theh University of Leeds which rendered so s l o w l y. At this time, web sites were hand crafted using HTML in files.

I cannot recall when our telephone provider turned ISP offered us broadband to the home, saving blocking the telephone line. Somewhere not long after the turn of the Millennium our eldest son was using early wiki markup to author content for his school website. Somewhere we started creating teh tooling to change text into HTML code,

items.title: Entering the WordPress Era
items.text:
Personally, I am not an early adaptor of most technologies, and my adoption of WordPress is no exception. Our ISP had successively increased our broadband speed on regular occasions, and I had embarked on my MSc through the Open University. The course featured extensive use of the online forum for discussion purposes, but several of my cohort were also expressing themselves via blogging, and the blogging tool of choice was WordPress.In fact, our course Systems Thinking in Practice actively encouraged it.

And so it was that I followed several of my colleagues into creating content via WordPress. My piece about Removing Constraints in Computing mainly comments about hype cycles, but I would argue that the history of products like WordPress follow a similar evolutionary path determined by the lifting of previous technology constraints.

As internet browsers expanded their capability through the advent of javascript and extensions to the HTML specification, assisted by ever improving bandwidth to carry larger web page payloads, so the power of products like WordPress expanded to offer better writing and drafting support.

items.title: Wordpress Develops
items.text:
I would say that my history with WordPress has been a classic "It isn't you ... it's me". Follow the link to my site, and you'll see that my posting was very sporadic, and so it turned out that many times when I went to add an article that the WordPress structure and UI had changed, reflecting teh ever growing capabilities of web technologies. I found I was relearning WordPress often even though the added features were mainly accretive, it was the layout changes and drafting tool differences that I found dicerted my limited attention away from writing.

Along the way I did try using the desktop clients, but they too seeemed to be quite fluid.

items.title: Going our separate ways
items.text: As you could see if you follow the links, I haven't deleted my WordPress site, but I haven't updated it recently. For anyone wanting to create a web site, I still think that WordPress has lots going for it, especially teh ability to quickly theme the site

items.title: Welcome to Reflecting
items.text:
This section of the site contains a series of vignettes based upon my experiences drawn from a good many years working in and around computing.

My hope is that through recording these, maybe others who stumble across these missives may understand a little context and how the various stories herein made me feel both at the time and in retrospect. My aim is to record any lessons that I learned along the way, but whether I succeed is going to be another matter.

items.title: Through a Computer Science lens ...
items.text:
I was talking top a recent Computer Science graduate and we were comparing our study experiences. Thinking through the last 50 years of computing history, I drew a conclusion that in my day, Computer Science teaching was largely about ways of overcoming the constraints imposed by the technology of the day ... 16-bit CPU / 64k RAM anyone (and that's the larger departmental computing stuff)?. It's not wonder that we didn't have a lot of complex data structures, or implicit language data structures like Pythomn's dictionaries. Maybe the years have filtered some of memories I recall a lot of time spent studying mathematical methods a.k.a. 'ways to approximate big maths problems'.

Over the years we have had Moore's Law to thank for creating large compute architecture, which in turn have created spec to develop the technology infrastructures we rely on today: network access, graphical computing, databases, and the emergent property we don't like but have to not only endure, but by necessity respond to, cyber-security. Access to all of these technology foundations, made ubiquitous by open-source, leads to a modern computer science degree being far more about exploitation of an abundance of capability.
path: So where does industry hype come from?

items.title: Databases Then
items.text: An example for me of the differences between then and now is that my database course win spring of 1982 was taught from one of the very few textbooks available at thme that covered the new-fangled art of normalised data in tables. It's fair to say that state of the art at that time was largely in ISAM data stores, and any access to real code for table-based data was in the new, and very expensive, products from IBM or Oracle. Much of the course, and the exams, was based on deducing the logic of data normalisation.
path: So where does industry hype come from?

items.title: Contemporary Database Learning
items.text:
To be honest, I've not experienced any modern database teaching, but I receive frequent course details for commerical training, I see YouTube training and guides, and even access videos of University lectures on the topic.

If I were asked to teach "databases" I could cover programming in SQL; how to design and manage a plethora of available database products; or even comparative database technologies along the limes of Seven Databases in Seven Weeks. I suspect any university modules face a similar dilemma.

Hype-Cycle

When I mention "Hype-Cycle" in this post, my meaning is a business cycle driven by speculation around a technology
path: So where does industry hype come from?

items.title: Technology Advances = New Freedoms?
items.text:
In sharing my views of how periods of technology hype come about, let me air my view that it is rarely a new technology alone that drives a period of hype. In my experience, the factors that that create a hype cycle include:

  • A upgrade or development of an existing technology that
  • lifts a pre-existing constraint and combines with
  • some novel circumstances that
  • in combination serve the zeitgeist of that time, and then
  • is presented with a new name

I agree with this recent keynote speech by Richard Campbell that a key to hype cycles is that the factors in hype are not well understood, or to precis Campbell: "When people can be sold anything because they don't know better"

To summarise here - The technology alone doesn't drive a hype-cycle. Instead a combination of factors occurring at the same time drives a hype-cycle
path: So where does industry hype come from?

items.title: "We've been here before"
items.text:
Looking back at my university days, I sometimes say that we could have created what is in a mobile phone at the time ... it would just have been the size of two large lorries or more1, probably required a direct connection to an electricity supply to serve all of the power needs, and have needed the efforts of avery available programmer in the world at that time (probably not in truth, just an awful lot of programmers). When us older folks look at something being presented as new and say "That's not new, we've had that for a while" we'rer referring to the fact that the various component parts really are only developments of what has been before.

Over the intervening years,

items.title: Is Ai really anything new?
items.text: And there is nothing new about me saying that AI is nothing new. As many are saying, the study / development of Artificial Intelligence dates back over 60 years. The challenge, as I allude to in this post is that we develop within constraints, and it as those constraints are removed that we are able to take more steps forward. The wuestion about whether those stpes are good or bad is another matter

items.title: What is the purpose of an IT Architect?
items.text:
The irony here is that I have been working as an architect in IT for over 25 years, and yet when pushed I still couldn't tell you exactly what an architect in IT actually does, I can tell you from my experiences, but put a group of IT architects in a room together, and I would suggest that getting a consensus would be difficult.

Let me try and explain...
path: What is the purpose of an IT Architect?

items.title: What sort of "Architect"?
items.text: I've seen several attempts to define the types of architecture practice found in IT. All have had a common theme insofar that all were different. Yes, there have been degrees of overlap between formal definitions but the actuality of where "... rubber meets the road ... " shows a much wider diversity amongst definitions.
path: What is the purpose of an IT Architect?

items.title: So who creates these "forma" definitions, and why?
items.text:
I could go back into a history of IT architecture, but maybe I'll reserve that for another post. I could also give a cynical answer that the formal definitions tend to be made by folks who make money by defining them, but that isn't strictly true

It is fair to point to the certification bodies, who make their money from training, examining, and certifying people in architecture disciplines. I can see a form of value for people being able to show that they can learn material and reproduce it in an examination of some sort. To be able to test, you need to define what is to be tested. Different organisations who can make money from this service need to differentiate themselves, hence one source of variation.

But that isn't the only source of these differences. My own experiences working in public sector have been both helped, and hindered, by teh UK Civil Service defining career profiles for different types of architect working in GDAD. As a former manager trying to recruit, this framework helped to provide consistency and a career progression framework. However, as a contributor to developing a framework (in this case defining Business Architect roles), the approach was remarkably insular without considering the delivery a architecture services and practice holistically.

items.title: Nothing Changes
items.text:
Did I mention that I have been working in the IT industry for over 40 years? I guess it's something I tend not to mention .... much As I head towards retirement and (hopefully) quieter days, I feel I have earned the right to look at new developments in the world of technology and say, as many before m have: "There is nothing new".

To be fair, this isn't quite true, but I'll come to that at some point. However, for the most part of my career I have seen lots of instances of something new and shiny, maybe the "Best thing since sliced bread", yet oin inspection it has proved to be anything but. The many instances make for good topics to discuss over a suitable libation, but I'll start by looking at the general pattern.

items.title: The pattern of a Fad - or is it a "Hype-Cycle"?
The start
items.text:
It is difficult to find a starting point for any hyped technology, generally the concepts have been around for a long period before someone, somewhere puts it to novel use. It is that novel use that drives the hype for several reasons.

You maybe don't believe me, but try a couple of examples:

  • Big Data - came to wider attention when a Silton Valley start-up combined the performance of in-memory database, with a large data set of test posts harvested from a social media provider to show customer sentiment.

    The technology wasn't new, but larger memory devices made it economic to put data tables in memory. The availability of APIs by social media providers and the availability of high-bandwidth internet connections, made it possible to harvest textual data by hashtags on a scale never imagined

  • Cloud Compute - was made viable by maturing virtual machine software running on processors becoming available with multiple-cores able to process massive workloads, and again that internet bandwidth.

I could keep going bu that would create a litany that doesn't really help the case yet

items.title: Confused Messages
items.text:
I posit that the key to these periods of hype is the initial confusion that abounds, and fosters serious FOMO, firstly on teh part of supply-side who don't want to be seen as behind the curve, and then on the part of consuming organisations who may feel that there is competitive advantage at risk of being lost.

Hindsight, they say, is always 20/20, but for each period of boom, there has been a significant amount of mis-understanding around the real nature of any proposition and what it represents. My personal experience on the part of the big Data example above was being told of the power of understanding customer sentiment ... and that is as true today as it was then. What was either mis-understood, or maybe intentionally left out of teh conversations, was that to get the scale of data needed to do the content analysis required large populations of tech-savvy customers using Twitter to express their views.

items.title: The Same Story
items.text: This ia an adjunct to Confused Messages, and for every technology cycle I have experienced, it is that the same story is repeated by every vendor or advocate. This raises flags for me, if there is only a single example then is there enough experience to justify the claims being made.

items.title: News Articles
items.text:
Yes, I am focused on the Big Data example as it represents the clearest example

Let's continue this theme ... the articles I see in the press tend to also consistently peddle the same story, or limited set of use cases. Generally teh press coverage includes speculation about how the example could be applied elsewhere, and it is this speculation that often gets mis-interpreted as additional use cases. Dif below the covers in these early stages, and generally you'll find yourself circling back to teh one and only real-life example.

items.title: Outcomes
items.text: Over time, some organisations are persuaded to try for themselves. Some can be successful, but others report difficulties and these get picked up and go through a second round of press attention.

items.title: Learnings
items.text:
So what have I taken away from experiences several of these technology fads? 1. If there are very few different examples of how to use it, then how do you know what it can really do? 1. If people blindly repeat the same story, then there isn't a base of experience to mine into 1. Ask questions

Sadly real0-life suggests that people focus on the sizzle, and don't question the current reality. And whilst teh sizzle sounds different ine each case, we do not appear to learn form any of these examples

Fad Sizzle IT Using the technology to deliver 'Information' DOT.COM You can save so much money as people will do it themselves online Enterprise Architecture. Save money by taking a holistic view Big Data See the sentiment of your customers Mobile Applications Customers can do anything at any time Robotic Process Automation Save money by having the computer do the work of people Cloud Computing Save money by letting someone else run your compute AI Save money by displacing people with Agents

So that';s me being grumpy. Maybe I'll write another post highlighting what we did learn

items.title: Unix days
items.text:
As a slow thinker it takes me a while, and a lot of reflection, to work many things out. Almost 50 years ago I started at University and met the Unix operating system then running, at my university computing debarment at least, on a 16-bit PDP-11.[^1} Whilst using it at the time, I didn't appreciate until many years later when working on porting Unix System 5 how the use of small, specific piece of software, and having the ability to join them together in differing ways to provide powerful tools worked so well.

Compare this to other operating systems at the time, for example VAX VMS as it was celled in teh eraly days, where an operating system utility could be hugely complicated with many parameters. One command-line instruction could be very powerful, but rather more stand-alone, a typical example of what I describe in my post aboutbloatware in software creating architectural problems

These days the flavour is Linux, and MacOS too, but that software architecture pattern of creating small, focused functional pieces of software, and joining them together stands today, and is still a good way ti create accretive functionality
